May 3, 2026 | Natural Disasters Summary

Buckeye, Arizona | USA - Hazen Fire rapidly spread across 270+ acres with flames up to 9 meters high; wildfire remains uncontained.

Parnitha, Penteli, Heraklion | Greece - Rare Arctic outbreak brought snow, freezing temperatures, hail, and strong winds across the country.

Albay (Camalig, Guinobatan, Oas) | Philippines - Mayon Volcano activity intensified with lava flows, ashfall, earthquakes, and pyroclastic flows affecting 100+ villages.

Hà Nội, Phú Thọ, Quảng Trị | Vietnam - Severe storms with hail and tornadoes injured people, damaged hundreds of homes, and devastated farmland.

Gaziantep | Turkey - Supercell storm with hail and torrential rain flooded streets, damaged infrastructure, and paralyzed traffic.

Tashkent | Uzbekistan - Intense rainfall caused urban flooding, submerged vehicles, metro flooding, and temporary power outages.

Yavan, Penjikent, Varzob | Tajikistan - Heavy rains triggered mudflows, damaging homes, roads, and infrastructure; a lightning strike killed one person.

data.raw_text:
USS Marblehead off New York, New York, United States, 6 May 1944.

The USS Marblehead (CL 12) had one of the most dramatic survival stories of the early Pacific war.

She was an Omaha-class light cruiser, commissioned in September 1924. By December 1941 she was an aging ship, already considered obsolescent, serving as part of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet based at Cavite in the Philippines under Admiral Thomas C. Hart. When war broke out, the Asiatic Fleet was vastly outgunned and was pushed south almost immediately. Marblehead withdrew to the Netherlands East Indies (modern Indonesia) and joined the hastily assembled ABDA (American-British-Dutch-Australian) command trying to hold the "Malay Barrier."

Marblehead was steaming as part of a striking force under Dutch Rear Admiral Karel Doorman, intending to attack a Japanese invasion convoy near Balikpapan, Borneo. Before they could close the range, the force was spotted and attacked by some 36 to 37 Japanese land-based bombers (G3M "Nells" and G4M "Bettys") flying from bases in Celebes. The Allied ships had no air cover.

Marblehead was hit by two bombs and badly shaken by a third near-miss. The damage was severe:

One bomb penetrated the forecastle and exploded below, starting major fires
Another struck aft and jammed her rudder hard over to port
The near-miss sprung hull plates and caused serious flooding forward
Fifteen men were killed, dozens more wounded

She was left burning, down by the bow, listing, and unable to steer normally, circling helplessly until her engineers managed to control her using only the engines (varying the speed of her port and starboard screws to crudely steer).

What followed is what made her famous. With no major Allied repair facility within reach in the collapsing East Indies, her crew had to nurse her thousands of miles to safety:

First to Tjilatjap on the south coast of Java, a small port with limited facilities, where temporary patches were made and the dead were buried ashore.
Then across the Indian Ocean to Trincomalee, Ceylon (Sri Lanka), still steering largely by engines.
From Ceylon around the Cape of Good Hope to Simonstown, South Africa, where the British drydock made more substantial repairs.
Then across the South Atlantic to Recife, Brazil, and finally up to the New York Navy Yard, arriving in May 1942, a journey of roughly 9,000 miles in her crippled state.

The story was widely publicized in the U.S. at a time when American war news was overwhelmingly grim, and Marblehead became a symbol of resilience and seamanship. Her captain at the time of the attack, Arthur G. Robinson, was awarded the Navy Cross.

After extensive repairs at New York (completed late 1942), she was deemed too old and slow for front-line Pacific service. She spent the rest of the war in the Atlantic, performing convoy escort duty, patrols in the South Atlantic out of Recife hunting blockade runners, and eventually supporting the invasion of southern France (Operation Dragoon) in August 1944, where she provided naval gunfire support along the French Riviera coast. She finished the war on training duties and was decommissioned in November 1945, then sold for scrap in 1946.

Her saga is often paired with that of her sister ship USS Houston (which was lost at the Battle of Sunda Strait a few weeks later) as bookends to the Asiatic Fleet's brief, doomed stand in the East Indies. Houston went down fighting; Marblehead, against all odds, came home.
